content.value: Determine the scope of fields, parameters, and block locals; resolve shadowed names; apply public and private access correctly.

Scope determines where a name is available. Fields are declared at class level. Parameters are available within their method or constructor body, and local variables are limited to the block in which they are declared. A nearer declaration can shadow a field with the same name. Use `this.field` in an instance context when necessary to identify the receiver’s field explicitly.

Access control answers a different question: whether code is allowed to use a member. Public methods are intended for clients; private fields and helpers belong to the class’s implementation. Private access is class-based, so a method may access private fields of another instance of the same class.

Inside setValue, the parameter shadows the field for the unqualified name value. `this.value` selects the field and receives the parameter’s value. In getValue there is no local value, so the unqualified name refers to the field.

Writing value = value in the setter assigns the parameter to itself and leaves the field unchanged. A local declared inside a block cannot be used after that block. Access modifiers do not replace the requirement to initialize local variables before reading them.
Add a local int doubled = value * 2 inside setValue and store doubled in `this.value`. Explain why doubled cannot be read from getValue and predict setValue(4) then getValue(): 8.
